people.name: Latanya Sweeney
people.roles: computer scientist · re-identification researcher · FTC chief technologist (2014)
people.place: Cambridge, Massachusetts (MIT, later Harvard); Pittsburgh (Carnegie Mellon)

keyWork.title: Simple Demographics Often Identify People Uniquely (Carnegie Mellon University, Data Privacy Working Paper 3)

people.contribution: As an MIT graduate student in 1997, Sweeney linked a $20 Cambridge voter list to Massachusetts state-employee health data released without names, and picked out Governor William Weld's hospital record. Her 2000 working paper estimated from 1990 Census data that 87% of the U.S. population was likely unique on five-digit ZIP code, gender and date of birth, and her 2002 k-anonymity model proposed a formal test for releases. She later founded Harvard's Data Privacy Lab and served as the Federal Trade Commission's chief technologist.
people.quote: In general, few characteristics are needed to uniquely identify a person.

people.influence: The Weld demonstration became the standard proof that removing names does not make data anonymous; an epidemiologist who later challenged its certainty still credits it with a profound impact on the de-identification rules of the 2003 HIPAA Privacy Rule.
people.thread: Her evidence that data stripped of names 'should not be considered anonymous' undercut the practice of sharing person-specific records without the person's knowledge on the strength of de-identification alone.

events.title: A graduate student finds the governor in 'anonymous' health data
events.place: Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Cambridge, Massachusetts
events.summary: Massachusetts' Group Insurance Commission had released patient-level data on about 135,000 state employees and their families, believed to be anonymous, to researchers and sold a copy to industry. Latanya Sweeney, then an MIT graduate student, bought the Cambridge voter registration list for twenty dollars and linked it on ZIP code, birth date and gender. Governor William Weld's record stood out: six Cambridge voters shared his birth date, three were men, and only he lived in his five-digit ZIP code.
events.significance: It showed that stripping names is not the same as making data anonymous, a lesson that shaped HIPAA's de-identification rules and every later argument that people need a say over data 'about' them.

sources.institution: International Journal on Uncertainty, Fuzziness and Knowledge-based Systems 10(5), 557-570 (author's copy, Data Privacy Lab)
sources.title: L. Sweeney, 'k-anonymity: a model for protecting privacy'
sources.quote: For example, William Weld was governor of Massachusetts at that time and his medical records were in the GIC data. Governor Weld lived in Cambridge Massachusetts. According to the Cambridge Voter list, six people had his particular birth date; only three of them were men; and, he was the only one in his 5-digit ZIP code.
sources.note: Same page: GIC collected data 'for approximately 135,000 state employees and their families. Because the data were believed to be anonymous, GIC gave a copy of the data to researchers and sold a copy to industry'; 'For twenty dollars I purchased the voter registration list for Cambridge Massachusetts'. The paper's reference for the voter list is dated February 1997.

events.title: ZIP code, gender and birth date: the 87% estimate
events.summary: In a Carnegie Mellon working paper, Latanya Sweeney used 1990 U.S. Census summary data to estimate how many people had rare combinations of demographic values. She found that 87% of the population (216 million of 248 million) likely had a unique combination of five-digit ZIP code, gender and date of birth, and about half (53%) on place, gender and date of birth. A 2006 re-analysis of the 2000 Census by Philippe Golle put the ZIP–gender–birth-date figure at 63%.
events.significance: The number turned 'anonymised' into a claim that had to be proved, and it is still the most-quoted statistic in arguments that personal data needs the person's own controls.

myths.claim: 87% of Americans can be identified from just their ZIP code, gender and date of birth.
myths.correction: Sweeney's 87% was an estimate from 1990 Census summary data of how many people 'likely' had a unique combination of five-digit ZIP, gender and birth date — not a count of people actually re-identified. Re-running the analysis on the 2000 Census, Philippe Golle found 63%. Actually naming someone also needs an outside list (such as a voter roll) that contains them; Barth-Jones argues that incomplete lists make many such matches uncertain. The core point — that a few ordinary attributes single out most people — survived the re-analysis.
